Teacher Resources: Start Here

This module is unpublished and only visible to course staff. It holds the teacher manual, syllabus, and setup notes for Digital Art Imaging 1, Semester 2 (Modules 3 and 4).

Course setup at a glance

  • Grading breakdown: Projects & Portfolio 60% · Classwork, Practice & Reflections 30% · Quizzes, Critiques & Discussions 10% (assignment group weights are already configured in this course).
  • Software: Pixlr E (free, browser-based), pixlr.com/e. No paid software required. Module 4 animation: frames are drawn in Pixlr E and assembled into a GIF in a free browser tool, taught tool-agnostically.
  • Portfolio convention: students keep all work in a OneDrive folder named DigitalArt_Portfolio_LastName; individual files follow DAI_W##_<Item>_LastName using the year-long week number (Module 3 = W19–W26, Module 4 = W28–W35).
  • Tier 3 project rubric (4 criteria, consistent every week a graded project is due): Understanding of the tools · Quality of choices · Craftsmanship · Intellectual honesty. Each project carries a native Canvas rubric scaled to its point value. The Module 3 Week 8 Typography Project uses its own capstone rubric (Hierarchy, Font pairing, Alignment, Expressive type).
  • Two-week projects: the Surrealism Collage (Module 3, Weeks 3–4) and the Digital Mosaic (Module 4, Weeks 2–3) are graded once, on the first week's assignment, which is due at the end of the second week. The second week's "Final" item is a 0-point completion checkpoint so students have a place to confirm the final upload.
  • Pacing: asynchronous with a live teacher for grading, office hours, and email support. Each module = 8 content weeks + 1 catch-up/flex week.

Files

  • Teacher Manual (PDF): full course orientation covering all four modules, weekly rhythm, grading, communication, and the live-adaptation table.
  • Syllabus 2026–2027 (PDF): student and family-facing syllabus. Add your name, office hours, and email before sharing.

Note: all auto-graded quizzes are multiple-choice or true/false with answer keys stored in the quiz itself. The Module 4 Week 2 Mosaic History reading check is a completion-credit survey with short-answer prompts; skim, do not grade for accuracy.

assignments.title: Practice: Masking in Pixlr E
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you build a full collage, practice the one skill that makes collage work: masking.

  1. Open pixlr.com/e. Create a new canvas.
  2. Bring in two images (your own photos, or provided practice images) as separate layers.
  3. Select the top layer. Add a layer mask and use it to hide part of that layer so the image underneath shows through.
  4. Change the top layer's blend mode (find this in the Layers panel, default is Normal) and try at least two options to see the effect.
  5. Take a screenshot of your Pixlr E workspace showing the Layers panel with your mask and blend mode visible.

Submit: Upload the screenshot.

Grading (completion):

  • Two images brought in as separate layers
  • A layer mask used to hide part of a layer
  • At least one non-Normal blend mode tried
  • Screenshot clearly shows the Layers panel

assignments.title: First Digital Collage
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Build your first full digital collage in Pixlr E.

Include all of these:

  1. At least three images (your own photos or provided practice images), each on its own layer.
  2. At least one layer mask used to blend or cut a layer into the composition.
  3. At least one blend mode other than Normal applied to a layer, chosen because of the effect it creates.
  4. A clear subject or idea: your collage should say something, even something simple, not just be images stacked at random.

Decide on purpose whether your seams will be smooth and hidden or visible and intentional, like the Dada artists you read about this week. Either is correct as long as it is a choice, not an accident.

assignments.title: Three Balance Sketches
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Practice seeing balance before you use it in a full composition.

  1. In Pixlr E, create a new canvas and place the same three simple shapes (use the Shape tool: for example one large circle and two small squares) on it.
  2. Duplicate your canvas (or start fresh) and arrange the shapes three different ways:
  • Symmetrical: mirrored around a center line
  • Asymmetrical: different sizes/positions that still feel evenly weighted
  • Radial: arranged around a center point
  1. Export all three as one image or three separate files.

Submit: Upload your three arrangements.

Grading (completion):

  • Symmetrical arrangement shown
  • Asymmetrical arrangement shown
  • Radial arrangement shown
  • Same three shapes used in all three

assignments.title: Balance
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Revise your Week 1 collage, or build a new short composition in Pixlr E, to clearly demonstrate one balance type: symmetrical, asymmetrical, or radial.

Include:

  1. The revised or new composition image, exported as PNG.
  2. A short written reflection (4-6 sentences) that:
  • Names which balance type you chose
  • Explains at least two specific changes you made to achieve it (size, position, color, or detail of specific elements)
  • Describes the feeling the balance type gives the piece (calm, energetic, focused, etc.)

assignments.title: Planning: One-Sentence Concept
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you open Pixlr E, plan your Surrealism Collage.

  1. Write your concept as one sentence: "A ___ where a ___ should be" (or a similar impossible combination).
  2. List the images you will need (your own photos, provided practice images, or a mix).
  3. Note which balance type (symmetrical, asymmetrical, or radial) fits the mood you want.

Submit: Type your sentence, image list, and balance choice directly in the submission box.

Grading (completion):

  • At least 3 images listed

Build a Surrealism Collage in Pixlr E: one clear, impossible combination built with intention and craft.

assignments.title: Self-Critique Checklist
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you share your collage with a classmate, look at it yourself. Open your Week 3 Surrealism Collage file and answer each item honestly (2-3 sentences each is enough):

  1. Is my Surrealist concept clear at a glance?
  2. Do my masked edges look intentional?
  3. Does my blend mode help the elements feel like they belong together?
  4. Does my balance still hold up after all my edits?
  5. Is my file free of stray layers or unintentional gaps?
  6. What is the ONE change I am making this week based on this checklist?

assignments.title: Surrealism Collage (Final)
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Submit your finished, revised Surrealism Collage. Use your self-critique and your classmate's feedback to make at least one real improvement before this final submission.

Include:

  1. Your finished PNG, flattened and exported at full resolution.
  2. Confirmation the file is saved to your portfolio folder as DAI_W21_Surrealism_LastName (same filename as your Week 3 draft; this replaces it).

Grading: Scored against the 4-criteria rubric introduced in Week 3 (Understanding of the tools / Quality of choices / Craftsmanship / Intellectual honesty). This is the single grade for the module's marquee project; Week 3's upload was a draft checkpoint, not separately scored.

assignments.title: Type Scavenger Hunt
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Type is everywhere once you start looking for it.

  1. Find one serif typeface in the wild: a book cover, a sign, a menu, a website.
  2. Find one sans-serif typeface in the wild.
  3. Take a photo or screenshot of each.
  4. Label each image: name the category (serif or sans-serif) and point to one letter where you can see feet (serif) or their absence (sans-serif).

Submit: Upload both labeled images in one document or as two files.

Grading (completion):

  • Correctly identifies one serif example
  • Correctly identifies one sans-serif example
  • Labels point to a specific letterform feature, not just a guess

assignments.title: Type Hierarchy Exercise
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Design a simple layout in Pixlr E that shows you understand hierarchy. Imagine you are announcing a school art event.

Include all of these:

  1. A headline (event name), largest and boldest text on the page.
  2. A subheading (date, time, or location), mid-sized, in a second color or weight.
  3. A body text block (2-3 sentences of details), smallest text, left-aligned for readability.
  4. Consistent spacing and alignment repeated across all three elements (rhythm).

assignments.title: Mood Matching Warm-Up
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Letterforms carry mood before anyone reads the words. Practice spotting it.

  1. Open Pixlr E's Text tool and type the word "ARRIVE" three times on one canvas, once each in three very different fonts from the font dropdown (for example: one bold and blocky, one thin and elegant, one rounded and playful).
  2. Under each version, label the mood it creates and one real product, movie, or event that font style would suit (for example: a fitness brand, a romance novel, a birthday party invitation).
  3. Export as a PNG.

Submit: Upload the PNG.

Grading (completion):

  • Three visibly different font styles used for the same word
  • Each version labeled with a mood and a real-world fit
  • Exported and submitted as a PNG

assignments.title: Art Lesson & Reflection: Expressive Type Poster
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Design a short poster or ad in Pixlr E that pairs an expressive headline with a readable body font, then reflect on the choices you made.

Part A: The poster. Pick a real or invented event, product, or show to advertise. Include:

  1. A headline in a display (expressive) font chosen to match the mood of your subject.
  2. A supporting line (date, tagline, or location) in the same display font at a smaller size, or in a second complementary font.
  3. A body text block (2-3 sentences of details) in a plain, readable body font, left-aligned.
  4. At least one warp, rotation, or blend mode adjustment applied to a text layer for expressive effect.

Use no more than three fonts total. Export as a PNG.

Part B: The reflection. In 4-6 sentences, answer:

  • What mood were you going for, and which font did you choose for the headline to create it?
  • Why does your body font contrast with your headline font instead of matching it?
  • What is one choice you would revise if you built this again?

assignments.title: Find Your Own Text-in-Art Example
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Charles Demuth is not the only artist to use letters or numbers as the main subject of a piece.

  1. Find one artwork, besides "I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold," where text or a number functions as a visual or compositional element, not just a caption or title. This can be a museum website, a book, or a search of a verified museum collection (a site ending in .edu, .org, or a named museum such as moma.org or metmuseum.org).
  2. Record the artist, title, and date.
  3. In 2-3 sentences, describe where the text or number sits in the composition and whether it reads more like a shape, a symbol, or a message.

Submit: A short text entry or a screenshot with your written description attached.

Grading (completion):

  • Names a specific artist, title, and date
  • Describes the text or number's role in the composition, not just that it exists
  • Source is a real, findable artwork

assignments.title: Text-in-Art Study
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Study how text or a number functions in a chosen artwork, then build your own small digital piece that does the same thing: makes a number or word a central, expressive part of the composition, not a caption bolted on afterward. Include all of these:

  1. A single number or word, sized and placed so it is the dominant shape in your composition (the first thing a viewer's eye lands on), built in Pixlr E.
  2. At least one supporting visual element (a color field, a shape, a background image, or a secondary text fragment) arranged around your central number or word, the way Demuth surrounded his numeral with city fragments and lettering.
  3. A deliberate typeface, color, and placement choice for your central text, not a default setting left untouched.
  4. Your name and the date, signed on the piece.

Then, in the submission text box, write a short artist statement (2-3 sentences):

  • What does your number or word represent, and why did you choose it?
  • Why did you place it, size it, and style it the way you did?

Before you build in Pixlr E, plan on paper. This check-in makes sure you have a plan before you spend time in the software.

  2. Sketch 2 to 3 small thumbnail layouts showing roughly where your headline, subhead, expressive element, and body text will sit.

  4. Photograph or scan your sketch page.

Grading (completion):

  • One-sentence message present and clear
  • At least 2 thumbnail layouts sketched
  • One thumbnail circled or otherwise marked as the plan going forward

assignments.title: Typography Project: Poster or Advertisement
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Design a finished poster or advertisement in Pixlr E that applies everything you have learned this module about type: hierarchy, font pairing, alignment, and expressive type.

  • A poster promoting a cause, club, or performance
  • A movie or book poster for a real or invented title

Include all of these:

  2. A subheading in a paired font that contrasts with the headline on purpose.
  3. A body text block (2 to 3 sentences), left-aligned, at least 16 pixels, for readability.
  4. One expressive typographic touch where the letters become a visual or compositional element (a curved or tilted word, type integrated with an image, an enlarged letter used as a shape).
  5. Consistent spacing and alignment repeated across the layout.

assignments.title: Value Scale Warm-Up
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you shade a full drawing, practice controlling value on its own.

  1. In Pixlr E, create a new canvas at 1200 x 400 pixels.
  2. Use the Shape tool to draw six equal rectangles in a row.
  3. Fill the first rectangle white and the last rectangle black.
  4. Fill the four rectangles in between with a smooth progression from light to dark, using gray fills or brush strokes at different opacities so the row reads as one continuous scale.
  5. Export as PNG and save to your portfolio folder as DAI_W28_ValueScale_LastName.

Submit: Upload the PNG.

Grading (completion):

  • Six values present, ordered light to dark
  • Progression is smooth, not random
  • File exported and saved to the portfolio folder

assignments.html:

  3. On your Line Art layer, draw clean final lines over your guides.
  4. On your Shading layer, render your subject with a full value range: highlight, midtone, core shadow, reflected light, and a cast shadow.
  5. Flatten and export as PNG.

assignments.title: Digital Mosaic
assignments.html:

Build a digital mosaic in Pixlr E. This project spans two weeks: plan and begin this week, finish and submit next week.

  3. Build your mosaic using either the tile-by-tile method (Shape tool, one tessera at a time) or the grid-overlay method (pixelate/mosaic-style filter on a base image, then refine by hand with the Shape tool).
  4. Keep a visible seam or gap between tiles so the piece reads as a mosaic, not a blurry photo.
  5. This week: complete your plan and place at least half your tiles. Next week: finish, refine, and export.

assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you submit your mosaic, critique it yourself using the four-step model: describe, analyze, interpret, judge.

  4. Judge: Does it succeed as a mosaic? Name one specific area you improved after this self-critique.

assignments.title: Frame Planning Sheet
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you draw a single frame, plan your animation.

  1. Choose one simple motion: a bounce, a blink, a wave, an object growing or shrinking, or something similar.
  2. Describe or sketch your 3 to 5 keyframes: what changes in each frame, and what stays exactly the same (unity).

  1. Choose one small, repeatable action for your loop: a bouncing shape, a blinking eye, a simple walk-cycle-style motion, or a growing/shrinking icon.
  2. Decide how many frames you will use. 4 to 8 frames is the target range.
  3. Sketch a box for each frame, in order, either on paper or in a simple document. In each box, rough out what is different from the box before it.

assignments.title: Animation Project

discussions.title: Combined Meaning

Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Think of a time you saw two images combined, in an ad, a meme, a movie poster, or an artwork, and the combination created a meaning that neither image had alone. In 4-6 sentences, describe the two images and explain the new meaning the combination created. Then reply to one classmate: Do you read their example the same way they did, or does the combination suggest something different to you?

Then find one classmate's post and give a full critique using all four steps: describe what you see, analyze how the elements work together, interpret the mood or idea, and judge whether it succeeds as a mosaic specifically (would it read clearly from a distance?). Write your critique in 4-6 sentences total, covering all four steps. Be specific and respectful; avoid "I like it" without reasoning.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (all four critique steps present, specific and respectful) = full credit
  • Thin (only 1-2 steps present, or vague) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Unity in Motion
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Find a short animation or GIF (from a website, app, or game). Link to it or describe it. In 4-6 sentences, identify one specific place where unity across frames is used well (the subject stays consistent while one detail moves) or one place where it breaks down (something shifts that should not have).

Then reply to one classmate: Add one additional observation about their example's timing or keyframes.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (specific example + unity correctly identified + reply) = full credit
  • Thin (vague example or missing reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Animation Peer Critique
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your refined draft loop. If your Canvas discussion allows file attachments, attach your GIF; if not, attach a link to the file in your OneDrive portfolio folder (set to viewable) or attach one representative frame plus a one-sentence description of the motion.

Then reply to at least one classmate's post using this three-part critique protocol from the lesson:

  1. What works: name one specific effective moment (a smooth section, a clear idea, a strong pose).
  2. What's unclear: name one specific moment that reads as rough or confusing (a jump at the loop point, a size change, pacing that feels off).
  3. One suggestion: offer one concrete, doable fix tied to what you named in step 2.

Do not write general comments like "nice job" or "looks good." Every part of your reply must name something specific. Write your reply in 4-6 sentences total, covering all three protocol parts.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (own post + reply hits all 3 protocol parts with specific detail) = full credit
  • Thin (reply given but vague, missing a part, or not specific) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Portfolio Showcase
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your finished portfolio (attach the file or a shared link) along with 2-3 sentences on which piece you are most proud of and why.

Then reply to one classmate, in 2-3 sentences: Name one specific thing you noticed in their portfolio: growth from early work to later work, range across different media, or a caption that stood out to you as strong. Be specific about which piece and what you noticed; do not just say "great job."

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (portfolio shared + specific pride statement + specific reply naming a piece) = full credit
  • Thin (portfolio shared but reply is vague or missing) = partial
  • Missing = zero
